rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to ensure all 10 compounds elute within 42 min while revealing the overall elution window and any severe co-elutions. This gives a strong first map of retention across composition without risking truncation.

All peaks eluted well within the gradient, so trim the solvent window to bracket the observed elution range and spend more gradient time where the peaks are. This should improve time efficiency while testing whether the critical mid-cluster gains or loses resolution under a narrower, shallower effective window.

The first run already had perfect resolution and the score is now limited by time, so the best next probe is a shorter version of that broad gradient to reduce run time. Comparing tG 10 vs 20 at the same phi window will also show whether the critical 6–7 pair is slope-sensitive or essentially unchanged.

The 10 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the central cluster, while 20 min gives full resolution but more time penalty; 14 min is a direct compromise likely to recover the 5–7 separations while keeping the run short. This will map how quickly the critical pair improves with slope and may land near the CRF optimum.

The critical 6–7 pair improves strongly as the gradient is lengthened, and 14 min is already close to optimal, so a small increase to 16 min is the most direct way to push that pair above the apparent scoring threshold while keeping time penalty at zero. This is the highest-probability local improvement around the current best method.

Since the 6–7 pair is the only remaining weakness and it is close to fully resolved at 14 min, temperature is the best lever to test for a selectivity gain without adding time penalty. A 5 °C decrease should slightly increase retention and may reorder or spread the close central pair enough to beat the current best CRF.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by collapsing a different central pair, so test the opposite direction: a modest increase to 45 °C may improve the local ordering around peaks 5–7 while preserving the favorable short runtime of the 14 min gradient. This is the cleanest remaining one-factor probe near the current optimum.

Temperature changes made the critical cluster worse, so the optimum is likely purely in gradient time near the 14–16 min region. Testing 12 min completes the local slope map on the fast side and can confirm whether 14 min is the true best or if the score plateau extends shorter.

All compounds elute far before the end of the gradient, so a slightly lower phi1 should compress the solvent window around the actual elution range without changing runtime, which may enhance selectivity in the central cluster. This directly tests whether the close 6–7 pair is helped by a narrower composition span rather than by longer time.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the limiting 6–7 pair and raised CRF, so continue in the same direction with a slightly narrower window. This is the most direct local refinement and could push that pair fully past the scoring cutoff while keeping the run short.

At phi1 = 0.85 the resolution term reaches 1.000 but incurs a small time penalty, so the best chance to improve on injection 9 is to keep the favorable narrower window and shorten tG slightly. This tests whether the 6–7 pair stays above the threshold while bringing run time back into the zero-penalty region.

The narrowed window at phi1 = 0.90 clearly helps the critical pair, and the 12 min version was too steep, so the next logical refinement is a slightly longer 16 min gradient. This should test whether full resolution can be achieved with this better selectivity window and whether the time penalty remains small enough to surpass the current best.

The best region is now clearly phi1 = 0.90 and tG = 14, so the remaining lever is subtle selectivity tuning by temperature around this narrowed window. Since 35 °C altered pair identities before, it is worth checking whether the combination with phi1 = 0.90 improves the central cluster rather than collapsing it.

With 35 °C worsening the cluster, complete the temperature check at the current best phi window by trying 45 °C. If the 6–7 pair has any favorable thermal selectivity at phi1 = 0.90, this is the last obvious route to exceed the current best without changing the promising gradient geometry.

Temperature has been unfavorable, so the remaining promising lever is the low-end composition window. Raising phi0 slightly while keeping the successful phi1 = 0.90 may redistribute the early part of the gradient and alter selectivity in the central cluster enough to improve the limiting pair without increasing runtime much.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved the score further, so combine that gain with the earlier observation that lowering phi1 toward 0.85 can fully resolve the limiting pair. This is the most promising local combination to try for a possible CRF of 1.000.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so use the remaining budget only to confirm how robust the optimum is in the most promising local direction. Lowering phi1 one more step tests whether the perfect score sits on a plateau or whether 0.85 is the edge of the optimum.

The maximum score is already achieved, so this run should probe robustness in the other promising direction by increasing phi0 while keeping the optimum phi1 and tG. This checks whether the perfect score persists on a broader plateau or whether phi0 = 0.10 is specifically optimal.

We now know the optimum includes phi1 = 0.85 and tG = 14 with at least some tolerance in phi0, so continue mapping the plateau upward in phi0. This tests whether still higher phi0 preserves the perfect score or begins to over-compress the first compounds.

A perfect-score plateau exists around phi0 = 0.10–0.15 with phi1 = 0.85, so test the adjacent corner at phi0 = 0.15, phi1 = 0.90 to define the high-scoring region more completely. This helps confirm whether the optimum is driven mainly by phi0, phi1, or their combination.

With CRF already at the maximum, use the remaining budget to test the nearest faster variant of a proven optimum. This checks whether the perfect-score region extends to a shorter gradient or if tG = 14 is the lower boundary for keeping the critical 6–7 pair fully resolved.

Since phi0 = 0.15 also gave a perfect score at tG = 14, test whether that slightly higher starting strength better tolerates a shorter gradient. This explores whether the perfect region extends toward faster methods at the other optimum corner.

The plateau at tG = 14 is established, and the faster 12 min variants lose resolution, so test the slower side at one optimum point to define robustness in tG. This confirms whether 14 min is the center of the perfect-score window or the minimum gradient time needed for full separation.

One perfect-score point exists at phi0 = 0.15, phi1 = 0.85, tG = 14, so use one of the final injections to define the slower boundary there as well. This completes the local robustness map around the optimum plateau without repeating any method.

With the optimum already secured at CRF 1.000, use the final run to probe the fastest nearby narrowed window that still showed strong selectivity at 14 min. This gives one last boundary point on how much gradient steepening and window compression the critical 6–7 pair can tolerate.
